newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Economic theorists win Nobel prize for human touch.
newsitem.headline: Economic theorists win Nobel prize for human touch.

text.p: Two researchers won the 1996 Nobel Prize for Economics Tuesday for considering how governments, companies and other institutions make tax policy and financial decisions with incomplete information.

Scottish Professor James Mirrlees, 60, of Cambridge University, and William Vickrey, 82, a Canadian, won the prize for their "contribution to the economic theory of incentives under asymmetric information" over 20 years of research.

The two economists focused on how governments, companies or any organisations cope with a constant lack of complete information -- so-called asymmetric information -- but still make strategic decisions.
The two men, who are not widely known in the economic world, have never met even though jointly their work has sowed the seeds of a new branch in economic theory.

"The importance of this prize is that the methodology can be applied in all kinds of contracts," Karl-Gustaf Lofgren, a member of the Nobel economic prize committee, said after the award was announced in Stockholm.
"This methodology has spread into textbooks of micro-economic theory. It is not very often you get new chapters in textbooks," he told Reuters.

The Nobel economics prize, which is one of six annual Nobel awards, was founded in 1968 to commemorate the 300-year anniversary of Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, and is awarded by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.
The two men will share the $1.12 million prize.

Jorgen Weibull, Nobel economics committee member, said Vickrey and Mirrlees' research was important for economists since it factored incentive, capability and social responsibility into the economic equation.
"Much of economic theory now centres on imperfect competition," Weibull told a news conference. "A lot of work is going on right now on extensions to this work."
Vickrey, in the 1940s, produced research on different types of auctions and a design for maximum economic efficiency.
But he also became known for his work on income taxation, rewriting the 19th century philosophy that all differences in income should be neutralised by taxation.
Vickrey said progressive taxation affected individuals' incentive to work and he reformulated the problem so that individuals' productivity should not be penalised by tax.

The Canadian-born economist, who is now Professor Emeritus at Columbia University, New York, was unavailable for comment immediately after the award was announced. He planned to hold a news conference later in the day.
Some 25 years later, Mirrlees built on Vickrey's work, mastering mathematical applications, simplifying the issue and applying it to other areas of economic theory.
He tried to find the optimum tax level by searching for links between levels of taxation and people's incentive to work.
Mirrlees said he first thought the telephone call from Sweden telling him of his prize was a hoax.
"It was extraordinary. My second thought was to check that the call was genuine," he said by telephone from his office at Cambridge.
But he did not rank the prize as the greatest day of his life. He said that came in 1968 "when I finally cracked the optimal tax problem. It came in a flash and it was very satisfactory.
"It was really exciting to solve a problem, a bit embarrassing to get a prize."
Mirrlees, who was born in Minnigaff, Scotland, said reading detective stories and other forms of mathematics were among his hobbies.
Economists singled out for praise the work that Mirrlees co-wrote in 1974 called "Project Appraisal and Planning."

"It became almost the bible for people looking to invest in developing countries," said Martin Weale, director of the National Institute For Economic and Social Research and an advisor to the British treasury.
Of Mirrlees, he said, "He's avoided macro forecasting so he's not as well known as some economists in this country but he is one of the country's leading economic theorists."
Weale described Mirrlees as a "slightly austere Scotsman but an extraordinarily nice person."
The Nobel Economic Prize was the third Nobel this year.
The literature prize was awarded on Thursday to Polish poet Wislawa Szymborska while Australian Peter Doherty and Swiss Rolf Zinkernagel won the medicine prize on Monday.
The winners of the physics and chemistry awards will be announced in Stockholm on Wednesday and the Nobel Peace Prize will be awarded in Oslo on Friday.
